feedback: If a learner draws bird → caterpillar or says the arrow means 'eats', re-label the arrow as 'is eaten by / energy goes to' and have them re-check that every arrowhead points toward the feeder.

If a learner describes 'who is connected to who' but cannot state a direction, they are ignoring arrowheads: reteach the directed-diagram convention (like a one-way street sign) — the arrowhead carries the meaning, not just the line.
When a learner can both read a given arrow correctly AND draw an unaided one pointing the right way, they have produced the convention, not just recognised it.
activities.intendedInsight: The arrowhead carries the meaning: it shows the direction energy/matter travels, from food to feeder — not 'this eats that'.
learnerActions: Look at a single arrow between two pictured organisms, e.g. grass → rabbit, and say exactly what it means: the arrow points to the eater, so energy/matter flows FROM grass TO rabbit.
Given 'a caterpillar and a bird that eats it', draw the arrow yourself, pointing the right way (caterpillar → bird).
Check every arrowhead in a small web points toward the feeder, re-reading each as 'is eaten by / energy goes to'.

Redraw a three-species chain with all its arrows reversed and decide whether it still makes sense — it does not, because energy would then appear to flow from the eater back to its food, the opposite of how feeding works.
activities.title: Lock in the arrow-direction rule first

feedback: If a learner can trace one chain but gets lost where an animal feeds two predators, scaffold by highlighting that one animal and following every arrow leaving it; the concept is present, only the diagram-tracing needs practice — do not reteach the arrow meaning.

In a web that shows every organism's food, a producer (a plant) has food arrows only leaving it and none arriving. Use this as a quick role-check, but confirm that it is a plant, because an animal whose food is not drawn would look the same.
activities.intendedInsight: A food web is many overlapping chains, and each organism plays a role (producer, primary consumer, secondary consumer, or decomposer if shown) that you can read from the diagram.
learnerActions: Start from one chain you can already read (grass → rabbit → fox); then overlay a second and third chain that share an organism, so the web grows from chains rather than appearing as a full tangle.

Name each organism's role: producers (plants, which make their own food using sunlight) and consumers; then split the consumers into primary consumers (eat producers) and secondary consumers (eat other consumers). If decomposers (e.g. fungi, worms, bacteria) are shown, name them as feeders on dead material and waste. Notice that a producer has no food arrows arriving at it, but check that it is a plant, because an animal whose food is not drawn in the web would also have only arrows leaving it.
Trace one chain end-to-end with a finger, saying the running label aloud (grass → rabbit → fox).
activities.title: Build the web up from chains and name the roles

feedback: If a learner assumes each organism belongs to only one chain, pick an animal that feeds two predators and trace both chains through it together.
Praise finding a node where multiple chains meet: this is the structural feature that makes a web more than a single chain.
activities.intendedInsight: Many organisms sit at the crossing point of several chains — a web is a mesh, not a set of separate lines.
learnerActions: Trace two different food chains that both pass through the same animal in the web.
Highlight one organism and follow every arrow that touches it to see how many chains cross there.
activities.title: Find shared organisms at crossing points
